theCountingProblem: HALF THE SOURCES NAME THE TEA ROOM AND HALF NAME THE HOTEL. Time Out writes 'The Palm Court at The Ritz' and 'Diamond Jubilee Tea Salon at Fortnum & Mason'; Olive writes 'The Ritz' and 'Fortnum & Mason'. Unmerged, the two most famous afternoon teas in London read as four weakly-supported venues. 45 aliases were needed and the count on 2+ went from 6 to 23. The canonical name is the one a reader books under, which is the hotel.

knownGaps: NO AWARD AND NO INSPECTORATE. Nothing in this topic has been judged by anybody, and there is no tier-A source at all - which is true of no other food topic on this site.

The article covers 22 tea rooms and the corpus reaches about half of them. Nine carry no citation, and each is marked 'named by no source in this corpus' in the article rather than quietly dropped. The verifier checks that absence is still true, because it goes stale the moment a source is added.
NO VIDEO TIER and NO COMMUNITY TIER.
openVenueQuestions: Café Rouge is named by two budget blogs and the chain has largely gone: its own site now lists ONE London branch, at St Katharine Docks, with the rest at Center Parcs. Worth saying rather than repeating a stale blog post.
'The British Museum' as a tea venue means the Great Court Restaurant, and 'The Melody Restaurant' is the one at the St Paul's hotel. Both are recorded under the name the sources use.

Nine of the article's 22 rooms have no citation: The Dorchester, The Lanesborough, Jumeirah Carlton Tower, Winter Garden, The Berkeley, The Stafford, The Milestone, One Aldwych and The Ampersand. They are in the guide on their own merits and the article says the corpus does not reach them.
